title: Which Song Ruled the Charts the Longest? You'll Never Guess!
summary: Have you ever wondered which song has stayed at number one the longest? It's not a summer jam or a dance craze—it's a Christmas song! Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You" has now spent 22 weeks at the top of the Billboard Hot 100. That's the most ever! The song first hit number one in December 2019, and it's jingled back to the top every holiday season since. Before Mariah broke the record, the longest-running number one was "Old Town Road" by Lil Nas X and Billy Ray Cyrus, which stayed for 19 weeks in 2019. Then Shaboozey's "A Bar Song (Tipsy)" tied that record in 2024. But Mariah's festive tune keeps adding weeks every year. Only about 4% of all number one songs have managed to stay on top for 10 weeks or more. It all started with Debby Boone's "You Light Up My Life" in 1977. Since then, only a few super-hits have joined the double-digit club. Boyz II Men's "End of the Road" lasted 13 weeks in 1992, and Whitney Houston's "I Will Always Love You" held for 14 weeks. Then Mariah and Boyz II Men teamed up for "One Sweet Day," which set a record of 16 weeks in 1995. That record stood for over 23 years! So next time you hear Mariah's classic, remember—you're listening to the longest-leading number one in history!
why_it_matters: This shows how a song you enjoy today could become a tradition that families share every year, creating a soundtrack for special moments.

background_read: The Billboard Hot 100 has tracked America's favorite songs since 1958. It counts radio plays, sales, and online streams to decide the ranking.
Christmas songs often return to the chart every December. Mariah Carey's hit was released in 1994 but didn't reach number one until 2019, showing how streaming can give old songs new life.

perspectives.description: Fans feel the song is a beloved holiday classic that deserves the record because it brings cheer to so many people.
Some wonder if holiday songs have an unfair advantage since they get a new boost every year, while other hits fade away.
Experts see this as proof that streaming changed how songs stay popular—old tunes can now break records decades after release.
